```text
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### Canonical RNA base pairs

The canonical Watson–Crick RNA pairs are A–U, U–A, C–G, and G–C.

### Codon adaptation index

For n included codons with supplied positive weights w₁,…,wₙ, CAI = (w₁ × … × wₙ)^(1/n), the geometric mean of those weights.

Choose an RNA probe and a matched escape controlpipeline.target_and_escapeChoose a target-specific RNA probe, then make a synonymous version of the target that no longer closely matches that same probe.

Choose an RNA probe and a matched escape control

Use the target and comparison CDSs to select the required probe by the probe-selection task’s rules. Keep that selected probe fixed while redesigning the target CDS as an escape control. The redesigned target must preserve its protein and meet the supplied mismatch minimum at every RNA window. The comparisons stay unchanged.

Practical context

This provides a sequence-level analogue of an RNAi target and rescue control: the original RNA matches the reagent, while a synonymous construct preserves the protein and disrupts that match. Actual knockdown and rescue depend on reagent activity; a mismatch threshold is only the design screen.

Method reference: RNAi-resistant rescue in a B-cyclin study.

Component tasks

Make the coding RNAdna.transcribe→Select a CDS-specific RNA probeassay.select_rna_probe→Match an RNA guiderna.guide_hits→Create a guide-escape controldesign.guide_escape

Task Outline

Inputs. cds: ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG TGA; background_cds_panel: ["ATG AAA GCA GTT TTC GTA CTG TGA"]; probe_length: 12; background_mismatch_floor: 1; escape_mismatches: 1; editable_positions: [6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21].

Procedure. First select the same target-specific 12-base probe as the probe-selection task. Keep it fixed, rewrite only permitted synonymous positions, and require every target window to have at least one mismatch to that probe’s reverse complement.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe": "AAAAUUGCUUUC",
  "escape_cds": "ATGAAAGCAATATTCGTACTATGA"
}

Prompt
## Task

Choose a target-specific RNA probe, then design a synonymous version of the target that escapes that same probe.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG TGA",
  "background_cds_panel": ["ATG AAA GCA GTT TTC GTA CTG TGA"],
  "probe_length": 12,
  "background_mismatch_floor": 1,
  "escape_mismatches": 1,
  "editable_positions": [6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21]
}
```

## Rules

- Use NCBI genetic code 11 for codon interpretation.
- First transcribe the original target and comparison CDSs and select a probe of exactly `probe_length` bases.
- The probe must be a perfect reverse complement of a target window. Every equal-length comparison-RNA window must differ from the probe’s reverse complement at at least `background_mismatch_floor` positions.
- Keep that selected probe fixed while designing the escape CDS. Check every equal-length window of the candidate coding RNA against the same probe’s reverse complement; each must differ at at least `escape_mismatches` positions.
- Only DNA positions in `editable_positions` may change. Preserve the original protein, DNA length, first codon, and terminal stop. Keep comparison sequences unchanged.
- Use ungapped comparisons and no wobble. If the selected probe has no valid escape design, return the specified failure object; do not switch to a different probe.

## Selection

First select the ASCII-lexicographically smallest probe meeting the original target/background requirements (A<C<G<U). Keep it fixed, then choose the lexicographically smallest feasible escape DNA (A<C<G<T). If that selected probe has no feasible escape, return impossible; do not try a later probe.

## Reference material

### Synonymous codons

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### RNA reverse complement

RNA complementary bases are A↔U and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write its complementary partner 5′→3′.

## Answer

- `probe` is the selected continuous uppercase 5′→3′ RNA sequence. `escape_cds` is the final continuous uppercase synonymous DNA sequence.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe": <RNA string>,
  "escape_cds": <DNA string>
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "probe": null,
  "escape_cds": null
}
```

First select the ASCII-lexicographically smallest probe meeting the original target/background requirements (A<C<G<U). Keep it fixed, then choose the lexicographically smallest feasible escape DNA (A<C<G<T). If that selected probe has no feasible escape, return impossible; do not try a later probe.

## Reference material

### Synonymous codons

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### RNA reverse complement

RNA complementary bases are A↔U and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write its complementary partner 5′→3′.

## Answer

- `probe` is the selected continuous uppercase 5′→3′ RNA sequence. `escape_cds` is the final continuous uppercase synonymous DNA sequence.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe": <RNA string>,
  "escape_cds": <DNA string>
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "probe": null,
  "escape_cds": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.

Encode a protein change and remove cloning sitesjoint.protein_edit_and_cloningIntroduce one requested amino-acid change and remove forbidden DNA sites with the fewest total base substitutions.

Encode a protein change and remove cloning sites

The requested mutation defines the target protein: one residue changes and all others remain original. Synonymous edits elsewhere are allowed to remove unwanted DNA sites. Search those choices together and minimize the total number of changed DNA bases, while preserving the fixed first and terminal stop codons. This differs from freezing the locally cheapest codon change before attempting cleanup.

Practical context

This turns a requested amino-acid change into a construct compatible with a chosen assembly method. The final translation checks the desired mutation, while motif checks ensure that unwanted restriction sites were not retained or created by the edits.

Method references: GoldenMutagenesis domestication, Site-directed mutagenesis protocol.

Component tasks

Encode a requested amino-acid substitutionconstruct.minimal_aa_edit+Remove specified DNA motifsdesign.remove_dna_motifs+Translate DNA to proteincds.translate

Task Outline

Inputs. cds: ATG AAA GAT TTC TTC GTA CTG TGA; residue_index: 3; target_aa: E; forbidden_patterns: ["GAATTC"]; strand_mode: both.

Procedure. Replace Asp3 with Glu in the cloning substrate. GAA would create GAATTC with the next Phe codon; GAG makes the same requested Glu substitution without that site and with the minimum number of base changes.

Final answer:

ATGAAAGAGTTCTTCGTACTGTGA

Checking the answer. The final CDS must encode exactly the requested mutant protein, contain no forbidden sites, and minimize total changes with the stated tie-break.

## Task

Encode the requested amino-acid substitution and remove the forbidden DNA patterns using the fewest total nucleotide substitutions.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA GAT TTC TTC GTA CTG TGA",
  "residue_index": 3,
  "target_aa": "E",
  "forbidden_patterns": ["GAATTC"],
  "strand_mode": "both"
}
```

## Rules

- Change only the requested amino acid in the protein. Keep every other residue unchanged under NCBI genetic code 11.
- Synonymous DNA substitutions at other codons are allowed when needed to remove forbidden patterns. Keep DNA length, the original first codon, and terminal stop unchanged.
- Remove every overlapping or cross-codon forbidden IUPAC match under `strand_mode`.
- Count changed nucleotides across the entire final CDS, including synonymous changes outside the codon for the requested substitution.

## Selection

Minimize the total number of changed nucleotides permitted by this task; among equally minimal candidates, return the lexicographically smallest full DNA string (A<C<G<T).

## Reference material

### Synonymous codons

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### IUPAC DNA base sets

An IUPAC symbol permits any base in its listed set. Choices at different positions are independent.

```text
A=A  C=C  G=G  T=T
R=AG  Y=CT  S=CG  W=AT  K=GT  M=AC
B=CGT  D=AGT  H=ACT  V=ACG  N=ACGT
```

### DNA reverse complement

DNA complementary bases are A↔T and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write the opposite strand 5′→3′.

## Answer

- Return one continuous uppercase DNA sequence.

If no valid result exists, return:

```text
IMPOSSIBLE
```

The base minigene retains native codons 1–7 and the native terminal TGA. It is an engineered truncation, not the natural full-length gene.

Build a tagged construct, cleave it, measure productspipeline.tag_cleave_massAssemble a tagged CDS, translate it, simulate TEV cleavage, and calculate the mass of each resulting fragment.

Build a tagged construct, cleave it, measure products

The input supplies tag and linker DNA plus its placement. Assemble the construct by the stated convention, translate the assembled DNA, and cut the product at the benchmark TEV sites. Then calculate each fragment’s mass separately. This tracks both module assembly and the residues left on each side of cleavage.

Practical context

This follows an affinity-tagged construct through tag removal to expected product identity. Keeping track of the exact cleavage scar matters because the purified target’s sequence and theoretical mass can differ from both the original untagged protein and the full fusion.

Method references: Removal of affinity tags with TEV protease, ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Component tasks

Build a tagged protein CDSconstruct.tag_fusion→Translate DNA to proteincds.translate→Derive TEV-cleaved productsconstruct.tev_products→Calculate peptide massprotein.monoisotopic_mass

Task Outline

Inputs. cds: ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA; tag_cds: CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT GAA AAT CTG TAT TTT CAG; linker_cds: GGT GGT TCT; placement: N.

Procedure. Build the same His6–TEV/GGS fusion as tag_fusion, translate it, and cut ENLYFQ|G. Sum each fragment’s residue masses plus its own water molecule, rounding each fragment mass once.

Final answer:

{
  "cds": "ATGCATCATCATCATCATCATGAAAATCTGTATTTTCAGGGTGGTTCTAAAGCAATTTTCGTACTGAAAGGTTGGTGGCGCACTTCCTGA",
  "fragments": [
    {
      "peptide": "MHHHHHHENLYFQ",
      "mass_da": 1765.7644
    },
    {
      "peptide": "GGSKAIFVLKGWWRTS",
      "mass_da": 1791.9784
    }
  ]
}

Checking the answer. Check the constructed DNA, all cleavage-product sequences, and each fragment’s calculated mass.

Prompt
## Task

Build the tagged CDS, translate it, apply ENLYFQ|G cleavage, and return the constructed DNA plus every resulting peptide and neutral monoisotopic mass.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA",
  "tag_cds": "CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT GAA AAT CTG TAT TTT CAG",
  "linker_cds": "GGT GGT TCT",
  "placement": "N"
}
```

## Rules

- For N placement, assemble: original first codon + tag + linker + remaining original sense codons + original stop.
- For C placement, assemble: original sense codons + linker + tag + original stop.
- Translate with NCBI genetic code 11 and first-stop termination.
- Cut every exact `ENLYFQG` match as `ENLYFQ|G`; G stays on the downstream fragment.
- Calculate each unmodified fragment’s neutral monoisotopic mass independently, with free termini and one water per fragment.

## Reference material

### Annotated CDS initiation

The annotated first codon of an intact CDS encodes initiating methionine (M), even when its internal-codon assignment is different.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Monoisotopic residue masses

Use the following incorporated residue masses in Da. A free linear peptide has the sum of its residue masses plus one H₂O, 18.010565 Da.

```text
A=71.037114  C=103.009185  D=115.026943  E=129.042593
F=147.068414  G=57.021464  H=137.058912  I=113.084064
K=128.094963  L=113.084064  M=131.040485  N=114.042927
P=97.052764  Q=128.058578  R=156.101111  S=87.032028
T=101.047679  V=99.068414  W=186.079313  Y=163.063329
```

## Answer

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

```json

  "cds": "{{cds}}",
  "tag_cds": "{{tag_cds}}",
  "linker_cds": "{{linker_cds}}",
  "placement": "{{placement}}"
}
```

## Rules

- For N placement, assemble: original first codon + tag + linker + remaining original sense codons + original stop.
- For C placement, assemble: original sense codons + linker + tag + original stop.
- Translate with NCBI genetic code 11 and first-stop termination.
- Cut every exact `ENLYFQG` match as `ENLYFQ|G`; G stays on the downstream fragment.
- Calculate each unmodified fragment’s neutral monoisotopic mass independently, with free termini and one water per fragment.

## Reference material

### Annotated CDS initiation

The annotated first codon of an intact CDS encodes initiating methionine (M), even when its internal-codon assignment is different.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Monoisotopic residue masses

Use the following incorporated residue masses in Da. A free linear peptide has the sum of its residue masses plus one H₂O, 18.010565 Da.

```text
A=71.037114  C=103.009185  D=115.026943  E=129.042593
F=147.068414  G=57.021464  H=137.058912  I=113.084064
K=128.094963  L=113.084064  M=131.040485  N=114.042927
P=97.052764  Q=128.058578  R=156.101111  S=87.032028
T=101.047679  V=99.068414  W=186.079313  Y=163.063329
```

## Answer

- `cds` is the exact constructed continuous uppercase DNA sequence. `fragments` lists every nonempty final TEV fragment in N-to-C order, retaining repeats.
- `peptide` is its continuous uppercase amino-acid sequence. `mass_da` is its neutral monoisotopic mass in Da as a JSON number, rounded once to 4 decimal places with one water per fragment.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

```text
{
  "cds": <DNA string>,
  "fragments": [

    }
  ]
}
```

Design a codon library and verify its coverage

Prompt
## Task

Design a stop-free IUPAC codon covering every target amino acid, then report how many concrete codons encode each amino acid in its expansion.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA",
  "codon_index": 3,
  "target_residues": ["A", "G", "V"]
}
```

## Rules

- Choose a single IUPAC triplet for the selected internal codon. Its expansions must cover all `target_residues` and contain no NCBI genetic code 11 stop.
- Expand that same selected triplet into distinct concrete DNA codons, translate each with its ordinary internal meaning, and count how many encode each amino acid.

## Selection

Require target-residue coverage and no stops. Minimize extra amino-acid types, then the number of concrete codons, then the IUPAC triplet in ASCII order A<B<C<D<G<H<K<M<N<R<S<T<V<W<Y. Compare the symbols themselves, not their expanded nucleotide sets.

## Reference material

### IUPAC DNA base sets

An IUPAC symbol permits any base in its listed set. Choices at different positions are independent.

```text
A=A  C=C  G=G  T=T
R=AG  Y=CT  S=CG  W=AT  K=GT  M=AC
B=CGT  D=AGT  H=ACT  V=ACG  N=ACGT
```

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

## Answer

- `codon` is the selected uppercase IUPAC DNA triplet. `residue_counts` maps every produced one-letter amino-acid symbol to the number of distinct concrete codons encoding it in that triplet’s expansion.
- Include all positive counts, including amino acids outside target_residues. Their sum is the expansion size. These are codon multiplicities rather than probabilities or full-protein residue counts. A valid design is stop-free.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "codon": <IUPAC DNA triplet>,
  "residue_counts": {"<one-letter amino-acid symbol>": <positive integer count>}
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "codon": null,
  "residue_counts": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.
Expected answer
Final answer:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "codon": "GBA",
  "residue_counts": {
    "A": 1,
    "G": 1,
    "V": 1
  }
}

Native CDS: E. coli K-12 MG1655 trpL, locus b1265. Reference CDS: NC_000913.3, bases 1,323,038–1,323,082 on the minus strand. Protein: NP_415781.1.

Shared source record and original sequence. Retrieved 26 October 2026.

Assemble coding modules and locate junction motifspipeline.fusion_junctionJoin two CDS modules, find peptide-pattern matches in the fusion product, and map those matches to the fused DNA.

Assemble coding modules and locate junction motifs

Assemble the modules using the supplied linker and start/stop convention, then translate the fusion. Search the whole protein, including patterns formed across a module junction. Map each result to coordinates in the new fused CDS, not to the coordinate systems of the two original inputs.

Practical context

A fusion can introduce a peptide feature that neither module contains on its own. Checking across each junction and mapping a hit back to DNA supplies the information needed for a subsequent allowed repair, such as removing an unwanted protease site.

## Task

Fuse A–linker–B under the module-join rule, find every peptide-pattern match, and report its residue and fused-DNA intervals.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

```json
{
  "cds_a": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA",
  "cds_b": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG TGA",
  "linker_cds": "GGT GGT TCT",
  "pattern": "SGGSK"
}
```

## Rules

- Remove A’s terminal stop and B’s first codon, then concatenate the remaining A DNA, linker, and remaining B DNA. Keep B’s terminal stop.
- Translate the entire fused CDS with NCBI genetic code 11, ending at its first in-frame stop.
- Find every overlapping peptide-pattern match, including matches spanning the assembly junction.
- Pattern syntax: a letter matches itself; `X` matches any residue; `[set]` matches a listed residue; `{set}` excludes listed residues.
- Report DNA intervals in the assembled CDS’s coordinates, not in either source CDS’s coordinates.

## Reference material

### Annotated CDS initiation

The annotated first codon of an intact CDS encodes initiating methionine (M), even when its internal-codon assignment is different.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

## Answer

- `fused_cds` is the exact assembled continuous uppercase DNA sequence.
- Each match gives aa_interval=[first_residue, last_residue] in the fused protein and nt_interval=[first_base, last_base] in fused_cds, both with 1-based inclusive integer endpoints.
- Include all overlapping matches, sorted by protein start and then end. An empty match list is [].

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "fused_cds": <DNA string>,
  "matches": [
    {
      "aa_interval": [<first residue>, <last residue>],
      "nt_interval": [<first base>, <last base>]
    }
  ]
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.

  "fused_cds": "ATGAAAGCAATTTTCGTACTGAAAGGTTGGTGGCGCACTTCCGGTGGTTCTAAAGCAATTTTCGTACTGTGA",
  "matches": [
    {
      "aa_interval": [14, 18],
      "nt_interval": [40, 54]
    }
  ]
}

Design and verify an RNA-editing-dependent productpipeline.edit_dependent_productDesign a CDS that preserves the original protein before RNA editing and gives a specified protein after the supplied edits.

Design and verify an RNA-editing-dependent product

First find a permitted synonymous encoding satisfying the editing-dependent design task. Then verify two branches from that same candidate: ordinary translation must produce the original protein, and transcription followed by the supplied RNA edits and translation must produce the target protein. Returning both proteins makes the two requirements inspectable.

Exercise scope

ADAR-mediated RNA recoding is the biological inspiration for the revised A→G translation example. The two branches check the unedited protein and the product implied by the supplied edit. This audits encoding logic; it does not design an ADAR recognition site, guide, or editing reaction.

Method reference: Programmable editing by endogenous ADAR.

Prompt
## Task

Design a synonymous CDS that produces the original protein before RNA editing and the requested protein afterward. Report the DNA and both protein sequences.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

In an edit object, `replace` is `[first_base, last_base, new_text]`; an empty `new_text` deletes that interval. `insert_after` gives an original base boundary and `sequence` gives the inserted text. Apply all edits to the original coordinates, simultaneously.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA TCT ATT TTC GTA CTG TGA",
  "rna_edits": [
    {
      "replace": [7, 7, "G"]
    }
  ],
  "target_protein": "MKGIFVL",
  "editable_positions": [7, 8]
}
```

## Rules

- Only DNA positions in `editable_positions` may change. Keep length, the original first codon, and terminal stop unchanged.
- Before RNA editing, the candidate must encode the complete original protein under NCBI genetic code 11.
- Transcribe that same candidate and apply exactly the supplied edits using original RNA coordinates and RNA replacement text.
- Translate the edited RNA from its original reading origin to the first in-frame stop. Omit the stop symbol. The resulting protein must equal `target_protein`.

## Selection

Among all sequences satisfying every condition, return the lexicographically smallest full DNA string, comparing bases in the order A<C<G<T. This is a tie-break among feasible sequences, not a minimum-edit objective.

## Reference material

### Synonymous codons

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### Initiation of coding RNA

At the first RNA codon, UUG, CUG, AUU, AUC, AUA, AUG, and GUG encode initiating M under NCBI genetic code 11. If that first codon is not an allowed initiator, use its ordinary internal assignment.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal RNA codons

Each internal RNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
UUU=F  UUC=F  UUA=L  UUG=L
UCU=S  UCC=S  UCA=S  UCG=S
UAU=Y  UAC=Y  UAA=STOP  UAG=STOP
UGU=C  UGC=C  UGA=STOP  UGG=W
CUU=L  CUC=L  CUA=L  CUG=L
CCU=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAU=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGU=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
AUU=I  AUC=I  AUA=I  AUG=M
ACU=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAU=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGU=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GUU=V  GUC=V  GUA=V  GUG=V
GCU=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAU=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGU=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

## Answer

- `cds` is the selected continuous uppercase DNA sequence. `unedited_protein` is its translation before RNA editing; `edited_protein` is its translation after transcription and the supplied RNA edits.
- Protein strings are continuous uppercase one-letter amino-acid sequences, ending before the first in-frame stop. A zero-residue protein is the empty JSON string "".

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "cds": <DNA string>,
  "unedited_protein": <amino-acid string>,
  "edited_protein": <amino-acid string>
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "cds": null,
  "unedited_protein": null,
  "edited_protein": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.
Expected answer
Final answer:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "cds": "ATGAAAAGTATTTTCGTACTGTGA",
  "unedited_protein": "MKSIFVL",
  "edited_protein": "MKGIFVL"
}

Engineered trpL minigene: E. coli K-12 MG1655 trpL, locus b1265. Reference CDS: NC_000913.3, bases 1,323,038–1,323,082 on the minus strand. Protein: NP_415781.1.

The base minigene retains native codons 1–7 and the native terminal TGA. It is an engineered truncation, not the natural full-length gene.

The minigene has A3S (GCA→TCT). The supplied RNA edit sets base 7 to G; choose a synonymous Ser encoding so that this edit yields Gly. No naturally observed editing is claimed.

Shared source record and original sequence. Retrieved 26 October 2026.

## Task

Design a synonymous CDS that produces the original protein before RNA editing and the requested protein afterward. Report the DNA and both protein sequences.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

In an edit object, `replace` is `[first_base, last_base, new_text]`; an empty `new_text` deletes that interval. `insert_after` gives an original base boundary and `sequence` gives the inserted text. Apply all edits to the original coordinates, simultaneously.

```json
{
  "cds": "{{cds}}",
  "rna_edits": {{rna_edits}},
  "target_protein": "{{target_protein}}",
  "editable_positions": {{editable_positions}}
}
```

## Rules

- Only DNA positions in `editable_positions` may change. Keep length, the original first codon, and terminal stop unchanged.
- Before RNA editing, the candidate must encode the complete original protein under NCBI genetic code 11.
- Transcribe that same candidate and apply exactly the supplied edits using original RNA coordinates and RNA replacement text.
- Translate the edited RNA from its original reading origin to the first in-frame stop. Omit the stop symbol. The resulting protein must equal `target_protein`.

## Selection

Among all sequences satisfying every condition, return the lexicographically smallest full DNA string, comparing bases in the order A<C<G<T. This is a tie-break among feasible sequences, not a minimum-edit objective.

## Answer

- `cds` is the selected continuous uppercase DNA sequence. `unedited_protein` is its translation before RNA editing; `edited_protein` is its translation after transcription and the supplied RNA edits.
- Protein strings are continuous uppercase one-letter amino-acid sequences, ending before the first in-frame stop. A zero-residue protein is the empty JSON string "".

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "cds": <DNA string>,
  "unedited_protein": <amino-acid string>,
  "edited_protein": <amino-acid string>
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "cds": null,
  "unedited_protein": null,
  "edited_protein": null
}
```

Prompt
## Task

Use permitted DNA substitutions to change frame A’s peptide while preserving frame B’s peptide. Report the final DNA and both frames’ original and edited peptides.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

Coordinates and intervals are 1-based and inclusive unless a rule states otherwise.

`frames` lists frame A first and frame B second. Each record supplies its inclusive DNA interval and strand.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA",
  "frames": [
    {
      "interval": [7, 12],
      "strand": "+"
    },
    {
      "interval": [6, 11],
      "strand": "+"
    }
  ],
  "target_peptide_a": "VI",
  "editable_positions": [8]
}
```

## Rules

- Only DNA positions in `editable_positions` may change, through equal-length substitutions.
- Extract the same two annotated windows before and after the edit. Reverse-complement any minus-strand window.
- Use ordinary internal NCBI genetic code 11 meanings for every triplet, with no initiation override. Keep stops as `*` and continue translating after them.
- The final A peptide must equal `target_peptide_a`. The complete B peptide must remain exactly unchanged.

## Selection

Among all sequences satisfying every condition, return the lexicographically smallest full DNA string, comparing bases in the order A<C<G<T. This is a tie-break among feasible sequences, not a minimum-edit objective.

## Reference material

### DNA reverse complement

DNA complementary bases are A↔T and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write the opposite strand 5′→3′.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

## Answer

- `cds` is the selected continuous uppercase DNA sequence. `frames` contains exactly two records, "A" then "B", in supplied window order.
- `original_peptide` and `edited_peptide` are the full internal translations before and after the DNA change, retaining every stop as *. `changed` is true exactly when those strings differ.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "cds": <DNA string>,
  "frames": [
    {
      "frame": <"A" or "B">,
      "original_peptide": <amino-acid string, retaining stops as *>,
      "edited_peptide": <amino-acid string, retaining stops as *>,
      "changed": <boolean>
    }
  ]
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "cds": null,
  "frames": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.
Expected answer
Final answer:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "cds": "ATGAAAGTAATTTTCGTACTGAAAGGTTGGTGGCGCACTTCCTGA",
  "frames": [
    {
      "frame": "A",
      "original_peptide": "AI",
      "edited_peptide": "VI",
      "changed": true
    },
    {
      "frame": "B",
      "original_peptide": "SN",
      "edited_peptide": "SN",
      "changed": false
    }
  ]
}

Native CDS: E. coli K-12 MG1655 trpL, locus b1265. Reference CDS: NC_000913.3, bases 1,323,038–1,323,082 on the minus strand. Protein: NP_415781.1.

The two overlapping test windows are supplied annotations, not two natural genes. C8T changes frame A Ala→Val while preserving the overlapping frame B Ser codon AGC→AGT.

Build and audit a controlled synonymous panel

Design a panel in which each member meets its assigned coding-RNA CG count and all share the requested total number of G/C bases. Transcribe and measure each actual candidate, and compare its translated protein with the original. This connects design targets to independently checkable measurements.

Practical context

This prepares and audits sequences for a controlled synonymous comparison: protein identity and total GC stay fixed while CG count varies. Such panels can support experiments measuring RNA abundance or protein output. Independent measurements of each designed sequence distinguish achieved controls from merely requested ones.

Prompt
## Task

Create a synonymous CDS panel with the requested CG and GC counts, then report each member’s measured RNA CG count and DNA GC fraction.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

```json
{
  "cds": "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG TGA",
  "target_cg_counts": [0, 1],
  "gc_count": 6
}
```

## Rules

- Use NCBI genetic code 11 for codon interpretation.
- Keep the DNA length, complete encoded protein, original first codon, and terminal stop codon unchanged.
- All returned DNA strings must be distinct. Keep members in the same order as `target_cg_counts`.
- For each member, count all overlapping CG occurrences in its coding RNA, including those spanning codon boundaries. Its count must equal the corresponding requested value.
- Every full DNA sequence must contain exactly `gc_count` G/C bases.
- Report measurements from the final selected sequences. The GC-fraction denominator is the complete DNA length.

## Selection

Among complete feasible panels, choose the lexicographically smallest list of DNA strings: compare the first differing member using A<C<G<T. Resolve choices across the whole panel, including distinctness; do not choose each member independently.

## Reference material

### Synonymous codons

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### GC fraction

GC fraction is the number of G and C bases divided by the number of bases in the sequence being measured.

## Answer

- `members` follows target_cg_counts input order. Each cds is a distinct continuous uppercase synonymous DNA sequence.
- `cg_count` is its integer count of overlapping CG in coding RNA. `gc_fraction` is G+C bases divided by full DNA length, as a JSON number rounded once to 6 decimal places.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "members": [
    {
      "cds": <DNA string>,
      "cg_count": <nonnegative integer>,
      "gc_fraction": <number>
    }
  ]
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "members": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.
Expected answer
Final answer:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "members": [
    {

Template
## Task

Create a synonymous CDS panel with the requested CG and GC counts, then report each member’s measured RNA CG count and DNA GC fraction.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

```json
{
  "cds": "{{cds}}",
  "target_cg_counts": {{target_cg_counts}},
  "gc_count": {{gc_count}}
}
```

## Rules

- Use NCBI genetic code 11 for codon interpretation.
- Keep the DNA length, complete encoded protein, original first codon, and terminal stop codon unchanged.
- All returned DNA strings must be distinct. Keep members in the same order as `target_cg_counts`.
- For each member, count all overlapping CG occurrences in its coding RNA, including those spanning codon boundaries. Its count must equal the corresponding requested value.
- Every full DNA sequence must contain exactly `gc_count` G/C bases.
- Report measurements from the final selected sequences. The GC-fraction denominator is the complete DNA length.

## Selection

Among complete feasible panels, choose the lexicographically smallest list of DNA strings: compare the first differing member using A<C<G<T. Resolve choices across the whole panel, including distinctness; do not choose each member independently.

## Reference material

### Synonymous codons

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

### NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

```text
TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
```

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### GC fraction

GC fraction is the number of G and C bases divided by the number of bases in the sequence being measured.

## Answer

- `members` follows target_cg_counts input order. Each cds is a distinct continuous uppercase synonymous DNA sequence.
- `cg_count` is its integer count of overlapping CG in coding RNA. `gc_fraction` is G+C bases divided by full DNA length, as a JSON number rounded once to 6 decimal places.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "members": [
    {
      "cds": <DNA string>,
      "cg_count": <nonnegative integer>,
      "gc_fraction": <number>
    }
  ]
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "members": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.

From CDS collection to a minimal measurement panelpipeline.rna_probe_panelFrom a collection of CDSs, choose the smallest supplied RNA-probe set giving each coding RNA a distinct match signature.

From CDS collection to a minimal measurement panel

Transcribe each CDS and calculate which candidate probes have exact complementary hits in each RNA. Use that match matrix to choose a minimal distinguishing panel. Report the selected probe IDs and each CDS’s binary signature in the same probe order, so the claimed discrimination can be checked directly.

Practical context

This joins sequence screening to an economical measurement plan: derive probe-hit signatures and choose the smallest set that distinguishes the supplied RNAs. It addresses which measurements would be informative under exact matching; binding strength and real assay performance belong to a subsequent probe-design stage.

Method reference: NUPACK documentation.

Component tasks

Make the coding RNAdna.transcribe→Match an RNA guiderna.guide_hits→Distinguish CDSs with a probe panelassay.min_probe_panel

Task Outline

Inputs. cds_panel: ["ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA", "ATG AAA GCC ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA", "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGT ACT TCC TGA"]; candidate_probes: supplied table shown in the prompt.

Procedure. Select the same minimum distinguishing probe subset as min_probe_panel. In that selected ID order, encode a 1 for an exact complementary hit and 0 otherwise for each RNA in its original input order.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe_ids": ["trpL_A3_window", "trpL_R12_window"],
  "signatures": [
    {
      "cds_index": 1,
      "bits": "11"
    },
    {
      "cds_index": 2,
      "bits": "01"
    },
    {
      "cds_index": 3,
      "bits": "10"
    }
  ]
}

Checking the answer. All signatures must match sequence-derived hits, be distinct across CDSs, and come from a minimum-size panel.

Easy example · references supplied+
Prompt
## Task

Choose the smallest candidate RNA-probe panel that distinguishes every supplied CDS, and report their binary match signatures.

## Inputs

DNA inputs are 5′→3′ coding strands. Ignore whitespace between bases.

```json
{
  "cds_panel": [
    "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA",
    "ATG AAA GCC ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGC ACT TCC TGA",
    "ATG AAA GCA ATT TTC GTA CTG AAA GGT TGG TGG CGT ACT TCC TGA"
  ],
  "candidate_probes": {
    "trpL_A3_window": "GAAAAUUGCUUU",
    "trpL_R12_window": "AGUGCGCCACCA",
    "trpL_common": "ACCUUUCAGUAC"
  }
}
```

## Rules

- Transcribe each supplied CDS and use only the candidate probes.
- A probe hits an RNA if at least one equal-length window is its exact reverse complement. Use no gaps or wobble.
- Record one hit/no-hit bit per selected probe, in the selected probe order. Every input CDS must have a different bit string.

## Selection

Minimize the number of selected probes, then choose the lexicographically smallest sorted list of probe IDs. Compare complete ID strings in ASCII order.

## Reference material

### Coding DNA to RNA

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

### RNA reverse complement

RNA complementary bases are A↔U and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write its complementary partner 5′→3′.

## Answer

- `probe_ids` contains selected IDs in ASCII order. `signatures` has one record per input CDS in input order, with its 1-based cds_index.
- `bits` has one character per selected probe in probe_ids order: 1 for an exact complementary hit anywhere in that coding RNA, otherwise 0. All signature strings must be distinct.
- A valid empty panel has probe_ids=[] and bits="" in every signature.

Use exactly this structure. `<…>` marks a typed value; array items and map entries repeat as needed.

### Output structure

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe_ids": [<probe ID string>],
  "signatures": [
    {
      "cds_index": <positive integer>,
      "bits": <string of 0 and 1>
    }
  ]
}
```

If no valid result exists, return:

```json
{
  "status": "impossible",
  "probe_ids": null,
  "signatures": null
}
```

After any explanation, write `Final answer:` on its own line. Begin the raw JSON on the next line; it may span multiple lines and ends your response.
Expected answer
Final answer:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe_ids": ["trpL_A3_window", "trpL_R12_window"],
  "signatures": [
    {
      "cds_index": 1,
      "bits": "11"
    },
    {
      "cds_index": 2,
      "bits": "01"
    },
    {
      "cds_index": 3,
      "bits": "10"
    }
  ]
}

Engineered trpL derivative(s): E. coli K-12 MG1655 trpL, locus b1265. Reference CDS: NC_000913.3, bases 1,323,038–1,323,082 on the minus strand. Protein: NP_415781.1.

Panel order: native trpL, synonymous Ala3 GCA→GCC variant, synonymous Arg12 CGC→CGT variant. Candidate 12-base probes are designed reverse complements of native windows 4–15, 28–39, and 16–27.

Shared source record and original sequence. Retrieved 26 October 2026.

Reference material. Coding DNA to RNA, RNA reverse complement

Reference material

These definitions and lookup tables supply the biological information used by easy prompts. Each task links only to the entries it needs. Instance data and required benchmark conventions are given in both prompt variants.

DNA reverse complement+

DNA complementary bases are A↔T and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write the opposite strand 5′→3′.

Coding DNA to RNA+

The supplied DNA is the coding strand, written 5′→3′. Copy its bases in the same order, replacing each T with U to obtain the coding RNA.

Codon length+

A codon is a group of three consecutive nucleotides.

Residue-to-codon correspondence+

Each amino-acid residue is encoded by one consecutive codon. The initiating residue is residue 1; a stop codon encodes no residue.

NCBI genetic code 11: internal DNA codons+

Each internal DNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

TTT=F  TTC=F  TTA=L  TTG=L
TCT=S  TCC=S  TCA=S  TCG=S
TAT=Y  TAC=Y  TAA=STOP  TAG=STOP
TGT=C  TGC=C  TGA=STOP  TGG=W
CTT=L  CTC=L  CTA=L  CTG=L
CCT=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAT=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGT=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
ATT=I  ATC=I  ATA=I  ATG=M
ACT=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAT=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGT=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GTT=V  GTC=V  GTA=V  GTG=V
GCT=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAT=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGT=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
Annotated CDS initiation+

The annotated first codon of an intact CDS encodes initiating methionine (M), even when its internal-codon assignment is different.

NCBI genetic code 11: allowed DNA starts+

The allowed annotated initiation codons are TTG, CTG, ATT, ATC, ATA, ATG, and GTG.

NCBI genetic code 11: DNA stop codons+

The DNA stop codons are TAA, TAG, and TGA. All other unambiguous DNA codons are sense codons.

NCBI genetic code 11: internal RNA codons+

Each internal RNA codon is an aligned group of three bases. The table gives its one-letter amino-acid assignment; STOP marks a stop signal.

UUU=F  UUC=F  UUA=L  UUG=L
UCU=S  UCC=S  UCA=S  UCG=S
UAU=Y  UAC=Y  UAA=STOP  UAG=STOP
UGU=C  UGC=C  UGA=STOP  UGG=W
CUU=L  CUC=L  CUA=L  CUG=L
CCU=P  CCC=P  CCA=P  CCG=P
CAU=H  CAC=H  CAA=Q  CAG=Q
CGU=R  CGC=R  CGA=R  CGG=R
AUU=I  AUC=I  AUA=I  AUG=M
ACU=T  ACC=T  ACA=T  ACG=T
AAU=N  AAC=N  AAA=K  AAG=K
AGU=S  AGC=S  AGA=R  AGG=R
GUU=V  GUC=V  GUA=V  GUG=V
GCU=A  GCC=A  GCA=A  GCG=A
GAU=D  GAC=D  GAA=E  GAG=E
GGU=G  GGC=G  GGA=G  GGG=G
Initiation after DNA editing+

At the first DNA codon, TTG, CTG, ATT, ATC, ATA, ATG, and GTG encode initiating M under NCBI genetic code 11. If the first edited codon is not one of these initiators, use its ordinary internal assignment.

Initiation of coding RNA+

At the first RNA codon, UUG, CUG, AUU, AUC, AUA, AUG, and GUG encode initiating M under NCBI genetic code 11. If that first codon is not an allowed initiator, use its ordinary internal assignment.

IUPAC DNA base sets+

An IUPAC symbol permits any base in its listed set. Choices at different positions are independent.

A=A  C=C  G=G  T=T
R=AG  Y=CT  S=CG  W=AT  K=GT  M=AC
B=CGT  D=AGT  H=ACT  V=ACG  N=ACGT
Synonymous codons+

Synonymous codons encode the same amino acid. Replacing a codon with a synonymous codon preserves that residue in the protein.

GC fraction+

GC fraction is the number of G and C bases divided by the number of bases in the sequence being measured.

Codon adaptation index+

For n included codons with supplied positive weights w₁,…,wₙ, CAI = (w₁ × … × wₙ)^(1/n), the geometric mean of those weights.

Canonical RNA base pairs+

The canonical Watson–Crick RNA pairs are A–U, U–A, C–G, and G–C.

RNA reverse complement+

RNA complementary bases are A↔U and C↔G. Complement each base, then reverse the sequence to write its complementary partner 5′→3′.

Dot-bracket notation+

Matching parentheses mark paired RNA positions; a dot marks an unpaired position. Each closing parenthesis pairs with the most recent unmatched opening parenthesis.

Trypsin cleavage specificity+

Trypsin cleaves after K or R, except when the next residue is P. The K or R remains on the upstream peptide.

RNase T1 cleavage specificity+

RNase T1 cleaves RNA after G. That G remains on the upstream fragment.

N-glycosylation sequon+

The conventional N-glycosylation sequon is N–X–S or N–X–T, where X is any amino-acid residue except P.

Monoisotopic residue masses+

Use the following incorporated residue masses in Da. A free linear peptide has the sum of its residue masses plus one H₂O, 18.010565 Da.

A=71.037114  C=103.009185  D=115.026943  E=129.042593
F=147.068414  G=57.021464  H=137.058912  I=113.084064
K=128.094963  L=113.084064  M=131.040485  N=114.042927
P=97.052764  Q=128.058578  R=156.101111  S=87.032028
T=101.047679  V=99.068414  W=186.079313  Y=163.063329
Kyte–Doolittle hydropathy scores+

Use these Kyte–Doolittle residue scores. Whole-protein mean hydropathy is their arithmetic mean, counting every residue occurrence.

A=1.8  R=-4.5  N=-3.5  D=-3.5
C=2.5  Q=-3.5  E=-3.5  G=-0.4
H=-3.2  I=4.5  L=3.8  K=-3.9
M=1.9  F=2.8  P=-1.6  S=-0.8
T=-0.7  W=-0.9  Y=-1.3  V=4.2
Ionization and net charge+

A basic site contributes +1/(1+10^(pH−pKa)); an acidic site contributes −1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)).

Basic sites: the N terminus and K, R, H side chains. Acidic sites: the C terminus and D, E, C, Y side chains. Count each terminus once and each listed side chain once per residue occurrence; sum their contributions.

Sources and practical precedents

  • NCBI genetic code 11 — Codon meanings and annotated initiators.
  • INSDC feature-table specification — CDS annotations and nucleotide ambiguity conventions.
  • ExPASy PeptideCutter — Protease specificity models and their experimental limits.
  • DNA Chisel examples — Translation-preserving motif removal, local GC constraints, and codon optimization.
  • DNA Chisel specifications — Explicit sequence constraints, including codon choices and translation preservation.
  • LinearDesign — Joint optimization of codon adaptation and a thermodynamic RNA-folding objective.
  • ViennaRNA — RNA structure analysis using thermodynamic models; the benchmark’s pair-count and additive-score exercises use simpler rules.
  • Primer3 — Primer selection with melting-temperature, complementarity, and pair-quality criteria.
  • GoldenMutagenesis domestication — Silent removal of internal cleavage sites for Golden Gate assembly.
  • Twist gene-design resources — Synthesis complexity associated with sequence repeats, homopolymers, and GC extremes.
  • Codon Statistics Database — Comparative codon-usage statistics, including GC and third-position GC.
  • ExPASy ProtParam documentation — Protein composition, hydropathy, theoretical pI, and other sequence descriptors.
  • ExPASy PeptideMass documentation — Theoretical proteolytic digests and peptide masses for protein identification.
  • PROSITE N-glycosylation pattern — The sequon pattern and the distinction between a candidate site and actual modification.
  • Cytiva ion-exchanger selection guide — Protein charge, pI, operating pH, and ion-exchange resin selection.
  • RNA and mRNA sequence mapping by mass spectrometry — RNase digestion, fragment identification, and complementary mapping information for RNA characterization.
  • NUPACK documentation — Thermodynamic analysis and design of nucleic-acid structures and interacting complexes.
  • CHARMING — Harmonizing synonymous codon usage to reproduce a desired usage pattern.
  • Restriction-site markers in engineered alleles — An example of adding a silent restriction site to help identify a desired genome edit.
  • Origin and evolution of the zinc finger antiviral protein — A biological example of RNA recognition sensitive to CpG dinucleotides.
  • RNAi-resistant rescue in a B-cyclin study — Synonymous changes used to make rescue cDNAs resistant to the corresponding RNAi reagents.
  • Coding-sequence determinants of expression — A synonymous GFP library illustrates experimentally varying coding RNA while preserving the protein; it is not the benchmark’s exact CG/GC-controlled panel.
  • Site-directed mutagenesis protocol — Point mutations, deletions, and other explicitly designed sequence changes.
  • Addgene bacterial expression collection — Examples of protein-expression constructs with fusion and purification tags.
  • Removal of affinity tags with TEV protease — TEV-mediated tag removal and the resulting protein products.
  • SwiftLib — Degenerate-codon-library optimization for desired amino-acid coverage and manageable library size.
  • RNase T1: enzyme specificity and applications — Thermo Fisher’s enzyme documentation: guanosine-specific cleavage of single-stranded RNA; fungal origin and RNA-analysis uses.
  • EcoRI recognition and cleavage site — A real restriction enzyme recognizing GAATTC; cleavage is G/AATTC.
  • Kyte–Doolittle hydropathy scale — The original experimentally informed scale for displaying hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions of proteins.
  • Structural basis for microRNA targeting — Argonaute uses guide RNA base pairing to recognize target mRNA; a uniform mismatch count is a simpler benchmark rule.
  • Nussinov and colleagues: Algorithms for Loop Matchings — The 1978 dynamic-programming treatment of noncrossing base-pair matching, a historical foundation for simplified RNA-folding problems.
  • ApoB RNA editing: CAA becomes a stop codon — Experimental C-to-U RNA editing changes a glutamine CAA codon to UAA in apolipoprotein B mRNA.
  • The apoB-editing catalytic subunit is a cytidine deaminase — Identification of the enzyme chemistry underlying apoB RNA editing.
  • Programmable editing by endogenous ADAR — Primary research on ADAR-catalyzed adenosine-to-inosine editing. The benchmark’s translation-only example represents the recoding as A→G.
  • Synonymous mutations and restoration of mRNA base pairing — The rpsT study found that compensatory synonymous substitutions restoring predicted pairing could partly or fully restore fitness in some tested mutants.
  • NCBI CDKN2A annotation — p16INK4a and p14ARF transcripts share a second exon read in different frames, providing a concrete biological example of overlapping coding information.
  • Imaging individual mRNA molecules with labeled probes — Primary research on detecting mRNA through complementary oligonucleotide probes; assay chemistry and fluorescence are outside the benchmark.
  • His6-tagged protein purification — A laboratory teaching resource explaining binding of a six-histidine tag to nickel affinity material.
  • Ensembl calculated variant consequences — Rule-based annotation using codons and amino acids, with synonymous, missense, stop-gained, and frameshift consequence categories.

Evaluation design

Paired prompts, separate score axes

Each underlying instance gets easy and hard prompts with one shared answer and validator. Track reference support separately from sequence length, number of edits, constraint density, or search-space size. Keep tool access and token budgets matched.

Report canonical final-answer accuracy and answer-format compliance separately. A correct answer must match the normalized reference, including every requested field. Intermediate results may also receive diagnostic scores; a plausible explanation cannot rescue a wrong final answer.

Prevent sequence leakage

Split related sequence families before deriving tasks. Keep parent CDSs, homologs, recodings, mutants, RNA products, protein products, and composed examples in the same partition.

Hold out selected task combinations as a separate composition-generalization test. Do not use the exact intermediate sequences from a held-out composition to train its individual tasks.

Certify reference answers

Generate one canonical reference answer per instance, including every tie-break. Independently verify protein preservation, all constraints, and the required selection rule. Keep exact-search instances small enough to certify the chosen feasible or optimal answer, not just one witness.

A reference may say IMPOSSIBLE only after an independent solver certifies infeasibility. NONE means no qualifying readout exists. A search timeout establishes neither result.

Status of this proposal

This document defines candidate task types, prompt templates, and scoring rules. It does not claim that a dataset, reference implementation, solver, or benchmark score already exists.

Before release: generate instances, implement reference solvers and independent validators, verify canonical-answer uniqueness and easy/hard equivalence, and pilot task lengths and search limits. The illustrative examples have been checked; they are not a released benchmark dataset.
